R02-D-01: Adults watching a three-year-old serve imaginary tea to a row of stuffed animals tend to see one of two things. Some see a charming waste of time, a pause in the serious business of growing up that will be outgrown once the child can read and count; others see a rehearsal of adult roles, a small person practising to be a host. Both readings miss what is most remarkable about the scene, which is that to pour tea that is not there, the child must hold two descriptions of the world in mind at once: the cup is empty, and in the game the cup is full. She must keep the game's version from leaking into the real one, so that she does not actually try to drink, and yet follow its consequences faithfully, so that a toppled cup leaves the bear 'wet'. This double bookkeeping is the same machinery that underlies counterfactual thought, the ability to ask what would happen if things were otherwise. A child who reasons that the bear is wet because the tea spilled is tracking a causal chain inside a supposition. Planning, explanation and much of science rest on exactly this skill, since to decide whether a plan will work, or why a bridge failed, one must build a world that differs from the actual one in a single respect and then trace what follows. Seen in this light, pretend play looks less like a holiday from thinking than like one of its earliest training grounds. Some caution is nevertheless in order. That play and counterfactual reasoning draw on a shared capacity does not show that more play produces better reasoners; it may be that children who are already good at holding alternatives in mind simply enjoy pretending more. Nor does every game of make-believe involve careful causal tracking; much of it is repetitive and loose. The claim worth defending is narrower: pretence gives young children a space in which suppositions can be entertained without cost, and in which the rules that govern them can be tried and broken without anything real being at stake. That narrower claim has a practical edge. Well-meaning efforts to make early childhood more productive often convert free play into guided activities with stated learning outcomes. Some guidance helps, and an adult who joins a game and asks what happens next can enrich it. But a game that exists to deliver a lesson changes character, because the child who knows that a right answer is wanted stops supposing freely and starts guessing what the adult has in mind. What made pretence valuable, its freedom from consequence, is the very thing that the attempt to harness it is most likely to destroy.
R02-D-02: Few ideas about teaching have travelled as far, or met as little resistance, as the notion that each learner has a style. Some children, it is said, are visual learners, others auditory, others kinaesthetic, and each will learn best when lessons are delivered in the matching form. The idea is attractive for honest reasons: it seems to respect individual difference, it gives teachers something concrete to do with that respect, and it fits the everyday experience that people do prefer some ways of taking in information to others. The trouble lies in the step from preference to performance. That people report preferences is not in dispute. What the theory needs is something stronger: that a learner labelled visual will learn more from a visual lesson than from a spoken one, while a learner labelled auditory will show the reverse. Testing this requires sorting learners by style, teaching each group in both ways, and checking whether the advantage flips from one group to the other. When the claim has been tested in this demanding way, the predicted crossover has generally failed to appear. Learners tend, on the whole, to benefit from the same methods whatever label they carry, and whatever preference they would have reported if asked. What does seem to matter is the fit between the form of a lesson and the content being taught. A coastline is better learned from a map than from a description, whoever the learner is; the sound of a language is better learned by listening; a knot is learned by tying it. Here the mode is chosen for the material, not for the student. The same holds in reverse: a pupil who insists that she learns best by listening will not master the shape of a coastline sooner because it is described to her aloud, however vivid the description. A teacher who presents geography through maps is not catering to visual learners, but simply using the form in which geographical knowledge is most naturally held. None of this means that variety in the classroom is pointless. Moving between pictures, speech and activity can hold attention and can give a learner several routes back to the same idea. The objection is to the diagnosis rather than to the variety. Labelling a child as one kind of learner invites both the child and the teacher to treat the other channels as closed, and a child told that she is 'not a reading person' may come to believe it. The cost of the theory is not that it wastes a few lessons, but that it narrows expectations while appearing to widen them.
R02-D-03: Students and teachers share a reasonable-sounding rule: if learning feels smooth, it is going well. A chapter reread the night before an examination seems familiar, a set of problems practised one type at a time feels increasingly easy, and the growing ease is taken as proof of mastery. The rule is reasonable because in many activities fluency really does track competence. A pianist who plays a passage without stumbling has, in some sense, learned it. Yet in the specific matter of building knowledge that lasts and transfers, the rule is frequently misleading, and sometimes backwards. The reason is that the conditions which make performance easy during study are often not the conditions which make memory durable. Rereading produces familiarity, the sense of having seen something before, which is easily mistaken for the ability to recall it unaided. Practising one kind of problem in a block lets the learner apply the same procedure again and again without ever deciding which procedure the problem calls for, the very decision a mixed examination demands. By contrast, spacing study sessions apart, testing oneself instead of rereading, and mixing problem types all make study feel slower and more error-prone, and all tend to produce better retention weeks later. The effort of retrieving a half-forgotten fact, or of working out which method applies, appears to be part of what fixes it in memory. It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson from this, namely that harder is always better. It is not. A difficulty helps only when the learner can, with effort, overcome it; material pitched far beyond a student's grasp produces confusion rather than consolidation, and a test on something never learned teaches little except discouragement. The useful difficulties are those that call on processes the learner will later need, such as retrieval, discrimination and reconstruction, rather than obstacles that merely slow things down. Printing a textbook in a faint, awkward typeface makes reading harder, but there is little reason to expect it to make anything stick. The deeper problem is one of judgement. Because learners rely on how study feels, they systematically prefer the methods that serve them worst, and they are not foolish to do so: the costs of effortful methods are felt now, while their benefits arrive later and unannounced. Teachers face a similar temptation, since a lesson in which students struggle looks, to an observer and to the students themselves, like a lesson that has gone badly. Changing practice therefore requires more than information about which methods work. It requires a willingness to distrust a feeling that is usually reliable, in exactly the setting where it is not.
R02-D-04: A long tradition explains exceptional performance by talent: the chess master and the concert violinist are thought to have been born with something the rest of us lack. A body of research on practice has done much to unsettle this view. Those who reach the top of skilled fields, it turns out, have typically spent very large amounts of time not merely doing the activity but practising it in a particular way: working on specific weaknesses, at the edge of their current ability, with prompt feedback, usually under the eye of a teacher. Experience alone, on this account, is not enough. A person who has driven a car for twenty years has had a great deal of experience but has probably not improved since the first few, because ordinary driving involves no deliberate effort to get better. The strongest version of this view holds that practice of the right kind is not just necessary for expertise but very nearly sufficient, so that differences in accumulated practice explain most of the differences between the great and the merely good. Popularised as a rule that a fixed number of hours will make anyone an expert, it has an obvious democratic appeal. It is also, in that form, hard to sustain. Among people who practise a great deal, the amount of practice leaves much of the variation in performance unexplained, and the size of that unexplained remainder seems to differ across domains. Where the rules are stable and feedback is immediate, as in many games and sports, practice accounts for more; where outcomes are delayed and noisy, as in forecasting markets or judging which patient will recover, it accounts for less. This last pattern is revealing, because it suggests that what practice builds depends on what the environment can teach. Deliberate practice requires knowing, quickly and reliably, whether an attempt succeeded. A violinist hears a wrong note at once; a chess player can check a line against a stronger opponent. A financial analyst may wait years to learn whether a judgement was sound, and even then the outcome will reflect luck as much as skill. In such fields long careers can produce confidence without accuracy, and the hours a person has logged may say more about seniority than about expertise. None of this restores the old picture of talent as a fixed endowment that settles everything. The research on practice was right that expertise is built rather than found, and right that the manner of practice matters more than its sheer quantity. What it cannot do is deliver the promise sometimes made in its name, that anyone who puts in the hours will arrive at the same place. Starting points differ, the rate at which practice pays off differs, and some fields offer so little reliable feedback that practice in the demanding sense is barely possible within them.
R02-D-05: The familiar explanation of teenage recklessness is ignorance: adolescents take risks because they do not understand the dangers, or because they believe, in some half-formed way, that harm happens only to other people. If that were the whole story, the remedy would be straightforward. Teach young people the facts about speeding, drugs and unprotected sex, and their behaviour should improve. Schools and governments have spent heavily on precisely this remedy, and its results have often been modest. One reason is that the premise is weaker than it looks. When adolescents are asked, in a calm setting, to estimate the dangers of various activities, their answers are often not very different from those of adults, and by the middle teens many reason about risk in hypothetical cases about as well as their parents do. What distinguishes them is less what they know than what happens to that knowledge in particular situations. Decisions taken alone and at leisure look quite mature; decisions taken in the company of friends, under excitement, look very different. In laboratory games that reward bold choices, adolescents have been found to take noticeably more chances when they know their friends are watching, while the presence of an audience makes much less difference to adults. A plausible account of this pattern appeals to the uneven timing of development. The systems that make rewards, and especially social rewards, feel intense appear to become more responsive around puberty, while the capacities for restraint and planning continue to mature into the early twenties. For several years, then, the accelerator is more sensitive than the brake, and the gap shows most clearly when peers raise the value of a daring act. It should be said that accounts of this kind are easily overstated. Brains do not determine behaviour on their own, adolescents differ widely, and plenty of teenagers who are surrounded by friends behave with conspicuous care. If the account is broadly right, it has an uncomfortable implication for policy: the most effective interventions may be those that change the situations adolescents find themselves in rather than the beliefs they carry into them. Rules that limit the number of young passengers a new driver may carry, or arrangements that make the safe choice the socially easy one, work with the grain of adolescent decision-making rather than against it. The account also suggests a more generous reading of adolescence itself. A heightened sensitivity to peers is not simply a defect awaiting repair; it is part of what drives young people to leave the family, form their own alliances and try what their elders would not. The same disposition that makes a reckless dare attractive makes new friendships and new ideas attractive too.
R02-D-06: It is widely believed that there is a window for learning languages, open in early childhood and closed by adolescence, after which a new language can be studied but never truly acquired. The belief has some foundation. On average, people who begin a second language in early childhood end up closer to native-like command than people who begin as adults, and the difference is clearest in pronunciation: a late learner who has spoken a language fluently for decades will often still carry an accent that a child immigrant lost within a few years. What the evidence supports, however, is a slope rather than a window. The image of a door that slams shut at a fixed age is the part of the popular picture least able to survive scrutiny. Several things complicate the story that age alone is at work. Children and adults who move to a new country do not learn under the same conditions. The child is enrolled in school, surrounded for hours each day by speakers of the new language and given every incentive to sound like them; the adult often works among speakers of her first language, uses the new one for limited purposes and has an identity already settled in the old. When late learners are compared with early ones, these differences in the quantity and character of exposure travel along with age, and it is hard to tell how much of the outcome each explains. Where adults are immersed in the way children are, some reach levels that the stricter versions of the window theory say should be out of reach. It also matters what is being measured. Accent appears most sensitive to the age of first exposure, and some aspects of grammar, such as fine judgements about word endings, seem sensitive too. Vocabulary, by contrast, goes on growing throughout life in a first language and a second alike, and adults often learn the early stages of a new language faster than young children do, because they bring better memory strategies and a developed grasp of how languages work. A single critical period for language as a whole therefore looks less plausible than a set of different sensitivities, declining at different rates for different components. None of this makes early exposure unimportant, and a parent who can give a child two languages from the start gives something valuable. But the window image has costs of its own. It persuades adults that serious learning is no longer open to them, so that they invest less and expect little, and then treats the resulting modest achievement as confirmation. A more accurate picture, in which age makes some things harder and a few things much harder without closing the door at any fixed point, is less dramatic but more useful.
R02-D-07: For much of the twentieth century, average raw scores on intelligence tests rose steadily in country after country, so steadily that the tests had to be renormed at intervals to keep the average at one hundred. The rise, which came to be called the Flynn effect after the researcher who did most to document it, presents an awkward dilemma. If the tests measure intelligence and the gains are real, then our grandparents, scored against today's norms, would have been of strikingly low intelligence, and a substantial share of them would have fallen in a range we now associate with serious intellectual difficulty. That conclusion is absurd on its face, and it is worth saying why: those generations ran farms, businesses and governments, and nobody who knew them found them obtuse. If instead the gains are an artefact of testing, it is hard to see why the artefact should be so large, so persistent and so widespread. The way out begins with a closer look at where the gains occurred. They were not spread evenly across the tests. They were largest on tasks that ask for abstract classification and for the detection of patterns in unfamiliar material, and much smaller on tasks that draw on stored knowledge, such as vocabulary and arithmetic. Consider a person asked what a spade and a pair of shears have in common. She can answer that both are tools, or that one is used to dig the flower bed and the other to trim the hedge around it. The first answer earns credit; the second does not. Yet the second is not stupid. It reflects a habit of thinking about things in terms of their practical relations, a habit well suited to a life in which what matters about a spade is whether it will break the ground before the rain comes. On this reading, the twentieth century did not make people more intelligent in some general sense; it trained a particular style of thought. Mass schooling, work that deals in symbols rather than objects, and a culture saturated with categories and hypotheticals rewarded the habit of setting aside what things are for and attending to what kind of thing they are. The tests, built by people who had that habit, measured it well. Nor is the spread of the habit a trivial change, since it is precisely the habit that a world of written rules, formal classifications and hypothetical planning keeps demanding of the people who live in it. The gains are therefore real, since the habit genuinely spread, but they are not gains in a single underlying power that would make the average person of today a match for the most gifted minds of a century ago. This resolution is attractive, but it has a price that is not always acknowledged. If scores on the most abstract tests reflect habits cultivated by a particular kind of society, then the tests cannot be quite what they were often taken to be, a culture-free measure of raw capacity. They remain good predictors of success in schools and workplaces, but partly because those institutions demand the very habits the tests detect. It does not follow that the tests are worthless, or that differences in scores within a generation mean nothing; among people educated in broadly similar ways, scores can still capture real differences in how well they reason. What does follow is that comparisons across generations, and across societies with very different patterns of schooling and work, need to be interpreted with far more caution than a single number invites.
R02-D-08: The picture of the ageing mind that most people carry is one of steady decline. Memory falters, thinking slows, and the sharpness of youth gives way, from some point in early adulthood, to a long and gentle slide. The picture is not invented. On tasks that require rapid processing of unfamiliar information, such as spotting a target among distractors or holding several new items in mind while manipulating them, performance does fall with age, and the fall can be detected well before what anyone would call old age. But the picture has been assembled in a way that makes the decline look both steeper and more uniform than it is. Much of the early evidence came from comparing people of different ages at a single moment, a method that is quick and cheap and was therefore used widely. A group of seventy-year-olds tested alongside a group of twenty-five-year-olds differs from it in more than age: the older group grew up with less schooling, different work and less familiarity with the kind of test being given. Studies that follow the same people over decades tend to show later and gentler declines than such snapshots suggest, though they carry biases of their own, since those who stay in a long study are often healthier and more able than those who drop out. Neither method gives a clean view, and the honest summary is that some decline is real, while its timing and size are less certain than the familiar picture implies. More important, the familiar picture attends to only half of what changes. Knowledge of words, of facts, of how things usually go and how people usually behave, goes on accumulating well into later life, and on tests that draw on it older adults often outperform younger ones. Some researchers have gone further, proposing that part of the measured slowing reflects not failing machinery but a larger store: a mind that knows more words takes longer to find any one of them, much as a large library takes longer to search than a small one. The proposal is contested, and it cannot explain away every loss. It does, however, show that the same observation, a slower response, can be read as a symptom of deterioration or as a cost of accumulation, depending on what one assumes about the mind producing it. It would be a mistake to replace the narrative of decline with an equally simple narrative of wisdom, in which age brings a serenity and judgement that compensate for everything else. Older people are not uniformly wise, and losses in speed and working memory have real consequences, for learning a new technology, for instance, or for following a fast conversation in a noisy room. The more defensible view is that ageing changes the mix of a person's capacities rather than lowering a single level, and that whether the change amounts to a loss depends on the task. In a setting that rewards speed with novel material, the young will usually have the advantage; in one that rewards the recognition of familiar patterns, a wide vocabulary or an accurate sense of how situations tend to unfold, the advantage may lie the other way. A good deal of everyday competence, from running a household to reading the mood of a tense meeting, belongs to the second kind. A society that judges older minds only by the first kind of task will find decline wherever it looks.
